concept.name: Rho
concept.definition: Rho is the sensitivity of an option's price to a change in the risk-free interest rate: the partial derivative of option value with respect to the rate for the relevant term. Calls have positive rho and puts negative rho; it is the least-watched first-order Greek because short-dated option values are only weakly rate-sensitive.
concept.intuition: Rho captures that buying a call is partly a deferred purchase: higher rates make paying later more attractive, nudging call values up and put values down.
concept.mechanics: Rho = dV/dr, usually quoted per 100 basis points. In Black-Scholes, call rho = K*T*e^(-rT)*N(d2) and put rho = -K*T*e^(-rT)*N(-d2). Sensitivity grows with time to expiration, so rho matters mainly for LEAPS and for rate regime shifts; it also explains why call-put price differences move with rates via put-call parity.
concept.formula: Rho = dV/dr; Black-Scholes call rho = K*T*e^(-rT)*N(d2); put rho = -K*T*e^(-rT)*N(-d2).
concept.failure_modes: Rho assumes a single flat constant rate; real rate changes twist the discount curve, and in high-rate regimes the simplification in short-dated books hides real funding-cost effects. Box-spread and parity-based positions, whose entire economics are interest rate plays, cannot be risk-managed with a single rho number.
concept.misconceptions: Rho being 'small' does not mean rates are irrelevant: for long-dated options, a 1% rate shift can move prices by several percent, and rate-driven early-exercise incentives on deep ITM puts are a first-order effect.
concept.example: A one-year $100-strike call with rho 0.45 gains about $0.45 if rates rise from 4% to 5%, all else equal; the same rho is negligible on a one-week option.

citations.source: The Options Industry Council (OCC) — Understanding Options Greeks
